body: Arabic is written and read from right to left. There are 28 base letters; each connects to its neighbours according to a small set of joining rules, and many letters change shape based on whether they sit at the start, middle, end, or stand alone in a word.

Qaida Noorania, the classical Qur'an reading primer used across the Muslim world, opens with this exact list. The student first names every letter clearly and in isolation, before any vowel marks are added. The goal at this stage is simple: every letter should sound distinct from every other letter.

Pay particular attention to letter pairs that share a region of the mouth. ت and ط, د and ض, ذ and ظ, س and ص, and ه and ح are common confusions for new readers. Each pair includes one light letter and one heavy letter, and the meaning of words depends on getting them right.

drills.caption: Letters 1 to 14 (alif through saad).
drills.text: ا ب ت ث ج ح خ د ذ ر ز س ش ص

drills.caption: Letters 15 to 28 (daad through yaa).
drills.text: ض ط ظ ع غ ف ق ك ل م ن هـ و ي

drills.caption: Light vs heavy pairs. Train the ear on the contrast.
drills.text: ت  ط  /  د  ض  /  ذ  ظ

drills.caption: Throat and tongue confusions worth drilling separately.
drills.text: س  ص  /  ه  ح  /  ا  ع

lessons.summary: Twenty eight letters, each with its own articulation point and shape. Recognising them is the first step before any tajweed rule can land.

body: A single Arabic letter on its own carries only its consonant sound. To make a syllable, a vowel mark is placed above or below it. The three short vowels are: fatha (a small slash above the letter, sounding like a short 'a'), kasra (a small slash below, sounding like a short 'i'), and damma (a small comma-shape above, sounding like a short 'u').

In Noorania practice, the student reads each letter through all three vowels in order before moving on. ب becomes بَ بِ بُ. The pattern repeats for every letter of the alphabet. This drills both the vowel and the letter into muscle memory.
The vowels themselves are short: about one count each. Stretching them into long vowels comes later, when madd letters are introduced.

drills.caption: Baa with the three short vowels: ba, bi, bu.
Cycle the same drill through three more letters.
drills.text: تَ  تِ  تُ  /  ثَ  ثِ  ثُ  /  جَ  جِ  جُ

drills.caption: kataba (he wrote): three fathas in a row.
kutiba (it was written): damma, kasra, fatha.

lessons.summary: Three vowel marks give a letter its short vowel: fatha (a), kasra (i), and damma (u). Without them an Arabic letter has no vowel at all.

body: Tanween is written as two fathas, two kasras, or two dammas at the end of a word. The doubling adds an n-sound that is heard but not written: كِتَابٌ is read kitaab-un, كِتَابًا is read kitaab-an, كِتَابٍ is read kitaab-in.

Because the trailing n-sound is acoustically a nun sakin, every rule that applies to nun sakin (idhhar, idgham, iqlab, ikhfa) applies to tanween in exactly the same way. Once you have the four nun-sakin rules, tanween rides along.
When you stop on a word that ends in tanween, the doubled vowel collapses. كِتَابًا read in pause becomes كِتَابَا (a long open vowel). كِتَابٌ and كِتَابٍ in pause become كِتَاب (silent).

drills.caption: Same word with damma-tanween, fatha-tanween, kasra-tanween.
Tanween at the end of سَمِيعٌ behaves like nun sakin before ب.

lessons.summary: When a short vowel is written doubled at the end of a word, the letter is followed by an unwritten n-sound. Tanween is treated like nun sakin in tajweed.

body: Sukoon is the absence of a vowel. The letter is voiced but nothing is added after it: مَنْ is read 'man' (not 'mana'). The mark looks like a small circle, sometimes shaped like a head, placed above the letter.

Letters with sukoon are where most tajweed rules live. Nun with sukoon triggers the four rules of nun sakin. Mim with sukoon triggers its own three rules. The qalqalah letters (ق ط ب ج د) bounce when they carry sukoon. The madd letters become long vowels when followed by sukoon. So the entire science of tajweed is, in a sense, the study of what each letter does when it sits in this 'no-vowel' state.

When you stop at the end of a word, the final letter is read as if it carried a sukoon, regardless of what vowel was originally written on it. Recognising sukoon trains your ear for the moment a tajweed rule kicks in.

drills.caption: Three short words ending on a sakin letter.
Two sukoons inside one word: nun sakin then mim sakin.

lessons.summary: A small circle above a letter means the letter carries no vowel. The letter is pronounced cleanly, with no sound following it.

body: إِنَّ is read 'in-na'. The first nun is silent (sakin), the second nun carries a fatha. Because they share an articulation point, the two nuns merge into a single, slightly held sound. The same happens with every shadda: read it as one held letter, weighted twice.

When the doubled letter is nun or mim, the shadda automatically carries a two-count nasal hum (ghunnah). This is one of the most common tajweed rules in the entire Qur'an: every إِنَّ, every ثُمَّ, every أَمَّا holds a measured ghunnah on the doubled letter.

Shadda also activates madd lazim when it follows a madd letter (الضَّآلِّينَ holds the alif for six counts because the shadda on lam locks the madd in place). And shadda on a qalqalah letter at a stop produces the strongest qalqalah of all.

drills.caption: Three doubled letters that each hold a two-count ghunnah.
Doubled letters with no ghunnah (held but not nasalised).

examples.focus: إِنَّ. The shadda on nun is held with a two-count ghunnah.

lessons.summary: A small w-shape above a letter means the letter is doubled: a sakin form followed instantly by a vowelled form, run together.

body: There are three madd letters. A bare alif preceded by fatha gives a long 'aa' (قَالَ). A bare waw preceded by damma gives a long 'oo' (يَقُولُ). A bare yaa preceded by kasra gives a long 'ee' (قِيلَ).
The vowel and the weak letter must match. Fatha on a letter followed by alif gives madd. But fatha on a letter followed by waw or yaa with sukoon gives a diphthong (ay or aw), not a madd.

All long vowels in the Qur'an start at this two-count baseline. Every other madd rule (munfasil, muttasil, lazim) is just an extension of this baseline, triggered when a hamza or sukoon shows up in a particular position after the madd letter. Hearing the natural two-count length cleanly is the foundation for all of them.

drills.caption: The same letter with each long vowel: aa, oo, ee.
Three real Qur'anic words, one for each madd letter.

examples.focus: قَالَ. The alif after qaf is held for two counts.

lessons.summary: When a short vowel meets its matching weak letter, the result is a long vowel held for two counts. The three madd letters are alif, waw, and yaa.

chapters.subtitle: Letters, vowels, and sukoon, in the Qaida Noorania tradition
chapters.title: Reading Foundations

body: The word تجويد comes from the root ج و د, meaning to make something good or beautiful. In context, it means reciting the Qur'an in the way it was revealed to and recited by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

Tajweed has two parts. The first is theoretical: knowing the rules of pronunciation, prolongation, nasalisation, and the qualities of each letter. The second is practical: applying those rules through repeated listening and recitation under a qualified teacher.

Scholars classify the application of tajweed as فرض كفاية (a communal obligation) for the Ummah, and فرض عين (a personal obligation) on every reciter to the extent needed to recite without distorting the meaning.
This section walks through the most common rules you will encounter in the mushaf. Each lesson explains the rule, shows real ayahs where it appears, and uses Ayman Suwayd audio for focused examples.

examples.focus: وَرَتِّلِ ٱلْقُرْءَانَ تَرْتِيلًا. "And recite the Qur'an with measured recitation."

lessons.summary: Tajweed is the science of giving each Arabic letter its proper articulation point and characteristics during recitation of the Qur'an.

body: Begin with a sincere intention: the goal is not performance, speed, or showing skill, but preserving the words of Allah as they were recited.
Read in a clean state when possible, sit with calmness, avoid rushing, and give the mushaf and recitation session your full attention.
Good tajweed is not only sound mechanics. It is also humility, measured pace, listening carefully, and returning to correction without ego.

drills.caption: Start practice calmly before the first ayah.

lessons.summary: The classical learning path begins with the reciter's manners before it enters technical rules.

body: Istiadha is said before beginning recitation: أَعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ.

The basmalah is recited at the beginning of every surah except Surat at-Tawbah. Between two surahs, teachers commonly train multiple connection patterns: cut all, join all, cut before basmalah then join to the new surah, or join the previous ending to basmalah then cut before the new surah.
The important beginner rule is simple: do not accidentally make the basmalah sound like it belongs to the previous surah's final meaning.

drills.caption: Keep the refuge and basmalah distinct.

examples.focus: بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَـٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ. Practice a clean basmalah before the surah.

lessons.summary: Know when to say the refuge, when to say the basmalah, and how the basmalah connects between two surahs.

body: Tahqiq is the slow teaching pace. It gives every letter and rule clear space, useful when learning new makharij or correcting mistakes.
Tadwir is the moderate pace most learners should aim for in daily recitation: not stretched, not rushed, and still fully measured.
Hadr is faster recitation. It is only correct when the rules remain intact. Speed is not an excuse to drop madd counts, ghunnah, or clear letters.

drills.caption: Three speeds, one rule system.

examples.focus: وَرَتِّلِ الْقُرْآنَ تَرْتِيلًا. The standard is measured recitation, whatever the speed.

lessons.summary: Slow, moderate, and fast recitation all keep the same tajweed rules intact.

body: The right of a letter is what never leaves it: its articulation point and permanent qualities. The due of a letter is what happens because of context, like madd, ghunnah, tafkheem, tarqeeq, idgham, or ikhfa.
A clear error changes a letter, vowel, or meaning. A hidden error keeps the basic word recognisable but breaks a tajweed rule, such as shortening a madd or weakening a ghunnah.
This app should train both: first make the word correct, then make the recitation beautiful and rule-accurate.

drills.caption: Letter right first, contextual due second.

examples.focus: صِرَاطَ. Replacing ص with س is a clear letter error; weakening tafkheem is a hidden quality error.

lessons.summary: Each letter has a permanent right and a contextual due; mistakes happen when either one is lost.

body: Classical scholars identify seventeen articulation points distributed across five regions: the empty space of the mouth (الجوف), the throat (الحلق), the tongue (اللسان), the lips (الشفتان), and the nasal cavity (الخيشوم).

The throat alone is split into three zones: the deep throat (ء، هـ), the middle (ع، ح), and the upper throat (غ، خ). Mixing these is the most common beginner mistake. For example, pronouncing ع like ء turns the meaning of many words.

The tongue produces ten distinct points, ranging from the deep base (ق) through the middle (ج، ش، ي) to the tip (ل، ن، ر). The lips produce four letters (ف، ب، م، و), each with its own subtle position.

Knowing the makhraj is not optional decoration. It is the foundation that makes the rest of tajweed possible. A letter pronounced from the wrong place is a different letter, and the meaning of the verse changes with it.

examples.focus: صِرَٰطَ ٱلَّذِينَ. Contrast ص (heavy, tip-of-tongue with raised back) with س in other words.
أَعُوذُ. Listen for ع from the middle throat, not ء from the deep throat.

lessons.summary: Every Arabic letter has a specific point in the mouth, throat, lips, or nasal cavity from which it is produced.

body: The deepest throat produces ء and هـ. These letters should not be swallowed or pushed into the chest.
The middle throat produces ع and ح. These are often confused by non-Arabic speakers; ع is voiced and deep, while ح is breathy and unvoiced.
The upper throat produces غ and خ. Both are close to the mouth compared with the earlier throat letters.

drills.caption: Three throat zones, two letters each.
drills.text: ء هـ / ع ح / غ خ

drills.caption: Practice ع against ح with all three short vowels.
drills.text: عَ  عِ  عُ  /  حَ  حِ  حُ

drills.caption: Isolate ع, then lengthen only when a madd letter follows.

examples.focus: أَعُوذُ. Listen for ع from the middle throat.
أَعْطَيْنَاكَ. Release ع from the middle throat before the heavy ط.
ٱلْعَالَمِينَ. Keep ع voiced from the middle throat, not like ء.

lessons.summary: The throat has three articulation zones: deepest, middle, and closest to the mouth.

body: The deepest part of the tongue produces ق and ك with the upper palate, with ق farther back and heavier.
The middle of the tongue produces ج, ش, and the non-madd ي. The side and edge produce ض, one of the hardest letters to master.
The tip of the tongue handles many high-frequency letters, including ل, ن, ر, ت, د, ط, س, ز, ص, ث, ذ, and ظ.

drills.caption: Move from back tongue to tip tongue.
drills.text: ق ك / ج ش ي / ض / ل ن ر

examples.focus: صِرَاطَ الَّذِينَ. Tip-of-tongue precision matters in ص, ل, ذ, and ن.

lessons.summary: Most Arabic letters are formed by the tongue, across its base, middle, side, and tip.

body: The two lips produce ب, م, and the non-madd و. The lower lip with the upper front teeth produces ف.
The nasal passage is not a letter makhraj by itself except through ghunnah, the nasal sound attached to ن and م in several rules.
When practicing mim, ba, iqlab, ikhfa shafawi, and ghunnah, the front of the mouth and nose must coordinate without forcing the sound.

drills.caption: Lower lip, two lips, then nasal passage.

examples.focus: تَرْمِيهِم بِحِجَارَةٍ. Mim before ba uses the lips with nasalisation.

lessons.summary: The lips produce four letters, while the nasal passage carries ghunnah.

chapters.subtitle: What tajweed is and where its rules come from
chapters.title: Tajweed Foundations

body: After makharij, teachers move to sifat because two letters can leave nearby places but sound different because of their qualities. A letter is not complete until both its place and its qualities are correct.

Some qualities are permanent. For example, س always has safeer, the whistle-like quality, and ق always has isti'la, the raised heavy quality. Other qualities appear because of context, like qalqalah when ق ط ب ج د carry sukoon.
A beginner should first hear the big contrasts: heavy versus light, breathy versus voiced, stopped versus flowing, and soft versus sharp. These contrasts make later rules easier to understand.

drills.caption: Breath, voice, strength, and flow.
Light and heavy pairs that learners commonly mix.
drills.text: س ص / ت ط / د ض / ذ ظ

examples.focus: صِرَاطَ. ص is heavy and elevated, unlike the lighter س.
ٱلْفَلَقِ. ق has a strong raised quality and may also bounce when stopped on.

lessons.summary: Sifat are the qualities that ride on top of a letter's makhraj, such as breath, strength, heaviness, softness, and flow.

body: The main heavy letters are collected in خص ضغط قظ. They are always read with tafkheem, though the strength changes with the vowel and position.
Most other letters are light by default. A common mistake is letting a heavy letter make the whole word heavy, or letting nearby light letters weaken the heavy letter.
Practice the contrast slowly. The goal is not a louder sound. The goal is a fuller mouth position for the heavy letter and a clean return to lightness after it.

drills.caption: The always-heavy letters.
drills.text: خ ص ض غ ط ق ظ

drills.caption: Switch between light and heavy without changing the vowel.
drills.text: سَ صَ / تَ طَ / ذَ ظَ

examples.focus: صِرَاطَ. ص and ط are heavy, while ر and ت should not become muddy.
قَالَ. ق is heavy, but the following alif should stay smooth and measured.

lessons.summary: Heavy letters raise the back of the tongue and fill the mouth. Light letters stay thin and clear.

body: Ra is heavy when it has fatha or damma, and it is usually light when it has kasrah. This is the first rule to master.
Ra with sukoon looks backward. If the letter before it has kasrah and no heavy-letter exception follows, the ra is light. If the previous vowel is fatha or damma, the ra is heavy.
At a stop, ra can change because the final vowel drops. Always check the final read form, not only the written vowel.

drills.caption: Vowel changes first, then sakin ra.

examples.focus: الرَّحْمَـٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ. Ra with fatha is heavy.
رَاضِيَةً مَّرْضِيَّةً. Listen for heavy ra at the start and the softer context later.

lessons.summary: Ra can be heavy or light depending on its vowel, surrounding kasrah, and stopping position.

chapters.subtitle: Permanent and changing qualities that shape each letter
chapters.title: Letter Qualities

body: A madd letter is one of three: ا preceded by a fatha, و preceded by a damma, or ي preceded by a kasra. When no hamza or sukoon follows, the prolongation is exactly two counts, like one quick rocking of the hand.

This is the default state. A reciter who reads بَا for less than two counts is rushing the letter. One who reads it for four is over-stretching it. Natural madd should sound effortless, never dragged.
Because every Arabic alif, long-waw, or long-yaa starts with this two-count baseline, training your ear on it is the prerequisite for all the longer madds.

examples.focus: قَالَ. The alif after ق is held for 2 counts.
يس. Both the ي in يَا and the ي of سِين carry natural madd.

lessons.summary: The natural prolongation of a madd letter for two counts (harakat). It is the baseline length on top of which all longer madds are measured.

body: Madd Muttasil (المدّ المتّصل, "connected") happens when the madd letter and the hamza sit inside the same word. Holding for at least four counts is required by every well-known recitation. Hafs typically reads it at four or five counts.

Madd Munfasil (المدّ المنفصل, "separated") happens when the madd letter ends one word and the hamza begins the next. Hafs has the option of two, four, or five counts. Most reciters today choose four or five for consistency with muttasil.
A useful test: if you can pause cleanly between the madd and the hamza without breaking a word, it is munfasil. If pausing would split a word, it is muttasil.

examples.focus: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا. Munfasil between يَا and أَيُّهَا.
جَآءَتْهُمْ. Muttasil: the alif and hamza sit in one word.

fragments.caption: muttasil: madd + hamza in one word
munfasil: madd ends a word, hamza begins the next

lessons.summary: Permissible prolongation of four to five counts when a madd letter meets a hamza, within one word (muttasil) or across two (munfasil).

body: "Lazim" means binding or unavoidable. Unlike munfasil and muttasil, which arise from how words meet, madd lazim is built into the word itself and never changes length whether you stop or carry on.

It splits into two families. كلمي (word-level) madd lazim shows up inside ordinary words: a long alif followed by a shadda, for example. حرفي (letter-level) madd lazim appears in the disjointed letters at the start of certain surahs (like الٓمٓ), where the spelled-out names of letters end with three-letter shapes whose middles are madd letters with sukoon.
Six counts is the longest a single madd is held in any qira'a. Practice it slowly. The goal is a smooth, sustained tone, not a strained or pulsed one.

examples.focus: ٱلضَّآلِّينَ. The alif before the shadda on ل is held 6 counts (kalimi).
ٱلْحَآقَّةُ. Same six-count hold over the alif into the shadda on ق.
الٓمٓ. The middle ا of لَام and middle ي of مِيم each carry harfi madd lazim.

lessons.summary: The strongest madd, six counts, triggered when a sukoon or shadda follows a madd letter permanently, regardless of stopping or continuing.

body: Start from madd tabi'i: a matching vowel and madd letter with no hamzah or sukoon after it. That baseline is two counts.
If a hamzah comes after the madd, the rule branches into muttasil when it is in the same word and munfasil when it is in the next word.

If sukoon comes after the madd, the rule branches again. A permanent sukoon or shadda produces madd lazim, held for six counts. A temporary sukoon caused by stopping is treated as madd 'arid lissukun.
Use this map as the learner's checklist: identify the madd letter, look at what comes after it, then choose the count.

drills.caption: Name the branch before counting the hold.

examples.focus: ٱلضَّآلِّينَ. The alif enters the six-count branch because of the permanent shadda after it.
يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا. The hamzah starts the next word, so this is the separated hamzah branch.

lessons.summary: A single overview of how natural madd branches into the longer madd rules when hamzah or sukoon appears after the madd letter.

chapters.subtitle: Holding a vowel for a measured count
chapters.title: Madd Rules

body: "Idh-har" literally means "to make apparent." The ن stays itself: full, unmuffled, and without merging into what follows.

The trigger letters are exactly the six letters of the throat (حروف الحلق). A common memorisation phrase is أَخِي هَاكَ عِلْمًا حَازَهُ غَيْرُ خَاسِرٍ, where the first letter of each word covers all six.

Idh-har is the simplest rule of nun sakin and tanween: nothing changes. Recognising it correctly is what tells your ear that the next three rules (idgham, iqlab, and ikhfa) are deviations from this clean baseline.

examples.focus: مِنْ هَادٍ. The ن before ه stays fully clear.

fragments.caption: ن before ه inside a word

lessons.summary: When nun sakin or tanween meets one of the six throat letters (ء، ه، ع، ح، غ، خ), the ن is pronounced clearly with no nasalisation.

body: Idgham with ghunnah covers four of the six letters: ي، و، م، ن. Here the ن disappears into the next letter, and a two-count nasal hum (ghunnah) carries over the merge.
Idgham without ghunnah covers the remaining two: ل and ر. The ن again disappears into the next letter, but this time without any nasal residue. The merge is dry.
The trigger letter must be at the start of the next word. If ن sakin and one of these letters meet inside the same word, idgham does not apply (this is rare, and is read with idh-har instead).

examples.focus: مَن يَعْمَلْ. ن before ي with ghunnah.
هُدًى مِّن رَّبِّهِمْ. Tanween into م with ghunnah, then ن into ر without ghunnah.

lessons.summary: Nun sakin or tanween merges into one of six following letters, captured by the mnemonic يَرْمَلُونَ (ي، ر، م، ل، و، ن).

body: "Iqlab" literally means "to flip." The mushaf signals it with a small مـ above the ن or tanween, a visual reminder that the sound has changed even though the spelling has not.

The mechanics: lips touch lightly into a م-position without fully closing, hold the nasal hum for two counts, then release into the ب. Beginners often slam the lips shut and produce a hard م. Keep the touch soft so the ghunnah does the work.
Iqlab only happens when ب comes after the ن sakin or tanween, never before.

examples.focus: مِنۢ بَعْدِ. The ن flips into a soft hidden mim before ب.
لَنَسْفَعًۢا بِٱلنَّاصِيَةِ. Tanween before ب becomes a nasalised mim.

fragments.caption: ن flips into hidden م before ب
ن before ب inside a word

lessons.summary: Nun sakin or tanween before the letter ب is converted into a hidden mim with two counts of nasalisation.

body: Ikhfa is the middle ground. The ن does not disappear (as in idgham) and does not stay distinct (as in idh-har). Instead, the tongue prepares the position of the next letter, and a nasal hum bridges the two for two counts.

The fifteen trigger letters are everything that is not throat letters (idh-har), not يرملون (idgham), and not ب (iqlab): ت، ث، ج، د، ذ، ز، س، ش، ص، ض، ط، ظ، ف، ق، ك. Reciters memorise them with a famous fifteen-word verse beginning صِفْ ذَا ثَنَا.
The character of the ghunnah shifts subtly with each trigger letter, heavier before heavy letters (ص، ض، ط، ظ، ق) and lighter before the rest. Hearing the difference takes time and a teacher.

examples.focus: مِنكُمْ. ن before ك with concealed ghunnah.
أَنفُسَكُمْ. ن before ف with concealed ghunnah.

lessons.summary: Nun sakin or tanween before any of fifteen specific letters is partly hidden, neither fully clear nor fully merged, with a two-count ghunnah.

chapters.subtitle: What happens to ن with sukoon (or any tanween) before the next letter
chapters.title: Nun Sakin & Tanween

body: Idgham Shafawi (إدغام شفوي): when مْ meets another م at the start of the next word, the two merge into a single doubled م held with ghunnah for two counts. "Shafawi" means "of the lips," since both letters share the same makhraj.
Ikhfa Shafawi (إخفاء شفوي): when مْ meets ب, the lips touch lightly without full closure and a two-count ghunnah carries through. It mirrors iqlab in feel but with مْ in place of nun.

Idh-har Shafawi (إظهار شفوي): for any other letter, مْ is pronounced fully and clearly with no merging or hiding. The trickiest pair is مْ before و and ف, where beginners tend to over-soften the م. Keep it sharp.

examples.focus: لَهُم مَّا. Idgham shafawi: مْ merges into the following م.
تَرْمِيهِم بِحِجَارَةٍ. Ikhfa shafawi: مْ before ب with light nasalisation.
أَنۡعَمۡتَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ. Idh-har shafawi: مْ before ع stays fully clear.

fragments.caption: idgham shafawi: مْ merges into م

lessons.summary: Mim sakin (مْ) has three possible behaviours depending on what follows: merging into another mim, hiding before ب, or staying clear before everything else.
lessons.titleEn: The Three Rules of Mim Sakin

chapters.subtitle: Three rules govern مْ before the next letter
chapters.title: Mim Sakin

body: Anatomically, ghunnah comes from the nasal cavity (الخيشوم), not the mouth. You can confirm you are producing it correctly by gently pinching your nose mid-word: if the sound chokes off, the ghunnah was real.
Whenever ن or م carries a shadda, hold the doubled letter with two counts of ghunnah. This is independent of any other rule. It is a direct property of those two letters when doubled.

Ghunnah is the audible thread that ties many tajweed rules together. Once your ear locks onto its character, ikhfa, idgham with ghunnah, and iqlab stop sounding like separate phenomena and start sounding like variations on one nasal hum.

examples.focus: إِنَّ. The shadda on ن is held with a two-count ghunnah.
ثُمَّ. The shadda on م is also a two-count ghunnah.

fragments.caption: shadda on م inside a word

lessons.summary: A two-count nasal hum produced from a shadda on ن or م. It is the same nasal sound that lives inside idgham, ikhfa, iqlab, and the merged mim rules.

body: The strongest ghunnah is on noon or mim with shaddah. The letter is doubled, so the nasal sound is complete and obvious.
The next level appears in idgham with ghunnah, iqlab, and ikhfa. The nasal sound remains measured, but it is shaped by the next letter.

The lighter level is the original ghunnah naturally present in noon and mim when they are read clearly. It is there, but it should not be exaggerated into a full two-count rule unless a rule calls for it.
For practice, ask: is the noon or mim doubled, hidden, merged, converted, or simply clear? That answer decides how present the nose should be.

drills.caption: Move from strongest ghunnah to clear noon.
drills.text: نّ / مّ / مَن يَقُول / مِنكُمْ / مِنْ هَادٍ

examples.focus: إِنَّ. Doubled ن is the strongest practical ghunnah.
مِنكُمْ. Ikhfa keeps the nasal sound while the tongue prepares ك.

lessons.summary: Ghunnah is not one flat sound. Teachers train it by strength, from doubled noon/mim down to clear noon and mim.

body: Qalqalah Sughra (small): the qalqalah letter sits with a sukoon in the middle of a word. The bounce is short and clean, just enough to make the letter audible.
Qalqalah Kubra (large): the qalqalah letter falls at the end of a word that you stop on. The bounce is more pronounced because the letter has nowhere to glide forward.
Some scholars add a third level, Qalqalah Akbar, for a stop on a qalqalah letter that also carries a shadda, which doubles the bounce intensity. The mechanism is the same; only the strength differs.
A common mistake is adding a vowel to the bounce (saying "de" instead of a clean "d"). The bounce should be flavourless: the letter without any vowel attached.

examples.focus: يَخْلُقُ. The ق sakin in the middle is small qalqalah.
ٱلْفَلَقِ. Stop on ق at end of ayah for large qalqalah.
تَبَّتْ يَدَآ أَبِى لَهَبٍ وَتَبَّ. The final ب stopped on with a shadda is the strongest case (akbar).

fragments.caption: qalqalah kubra: stop on ق at end
qalqalah akbar: stop on ب with shadda

lessons.summary: The five letters ق، ط، ب، ج، د produce an audible bounce when they carry sukoon or are stopped on. Memorise them with the phrase قُطْبُ جَدٍّ.

body: Hamzat al-Wasl is what makes the alif of ٱلْحَمْدُ disappear when it follows another word. You say بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ as one continuous phrase, not bismi-i-llaahi.

Its purpose is purely phonetic: Arabic does not begin a word with a sukoon, so a connecting hamza is inserted to give the tongue something to start with. Once the next word arrives with its own vowel, the connector is no longer needed and falls away.

When you do start fresh on a hamzat al-wasl, the vowel it takes is determined by what follows: damma if the third letter has a damma (e.g. ٱنظُرْ), kasra if it has a fatha or kasra (e.g. ٱلْحَمْدُ becomes "al-"), or the original vowel for definite-article-like cases.

examples.focus: بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ. The alif of اللَّهِ is silent because we are continuing from بِسْمِ.
ٱلْحَمْدُ. Start fresh and the hamzat al-wasl returns as "al-".

fragments.caption: alif of اللَّه drops in continuation
starts with un- because third letter is damma

lessons.summary: A connecting hamza that is pronounced when starting fresh and silently dropped when continuing from a previous word.

body: There are fourteen sun letters: ت، ث، د، ذ، ر، ز، س، ش، ص، ض، ط، ظ، ل، ن. After ال, the lam disappears and the following letter is doubled with a shadda. الشَّمْس ("the sun") is the canonical example, and the source of the name.
The other fourteen letters of the alphabet are moon letters. After ال, the lam is pronounced with a sukoon and the next letter follows clearly. الْقَمَر ("the moon") is the canonical example.

A quick test for any word: look at the letter right after ال. If it carries a shadda in the mushaf, the lam is silent (shamsiyyah). If it has a sukoon on the lam itself, the lam is clear (qamariyyah).

examples.focus: وَٱلشَّمْسِ. Sun lam: the ل is silent, ش is doubled.
وَٱلْقَمَرِ. Moon lam: the ل carries a sukoon and is heard.

fragments.caption: sun lam: ل silent, ش doubled
sun lam: ل silent before ص

lessons.summary: The lam of "ال" either assimilates silently into the next letter (sun lam) or stays clear (moon lam), depending on the letter that follows.

body: The famous sun and moon lesson only explains the lam of ال. After that, learners still need to recognise lam sakin in verbs, nouns, and short particles like هل and بل.
The default is clear pronunciation when lam sakin is followed by most letters. The tongue touches its makhraj and releases without swallowing the sound.
When lam in a particle meets ل or ر in connected recitation, teachers point out the merge separately so the learner does not apply the sun-letter rule to every lam they see.
This page is mostly a recognition drill: identify which lam you are reading before deciding whether it is clear or merged.

drills.caption: Verb, particle, and noun lams.

examples.focus: قُلْ هُوَ. Lam of a verb, read clearly before ه.
قُلْ نَعَمْ. Another verb lam; do not treat it like the lam of ال.

fragments.caption: lam of a particle before another lam

lessons.summary: Not every lam belongs to the definite article ال. Lam also appears inside verbs, nouns, and particles, and those cases need their own attention.

chapters.subtitle: Ghunnah, qalqalah, hamzat al-wasl, and the lam of "al-"
chapters.title: Other Core Rules

body: م (waqf lazim): a necessary stop. Continuing changes the meaning, sometimes seriously. Always stop here.
لا (waqf mamnu'): do not stop. Continue to the next word; if you have already stopped, go back a word or two and continue from there.
ج (waqf ja'iz): permissible stop, neither preferred nor discouraged.
قلى (al-waqfu awla): stopping is preferred over continuing.
صلى (al-waslu awla): continuing is preferred over stopping.
ع (ruku' marker): a recommended stop at the end of a thematic section, traditionally used as a unit in tarawih.

When you do stop, the last letter is read with sukoon regardless of its original vowel. This sometimes triggers qalqalah kubra (if the letter is one of قطب جد) or alters a hidden hamzat al-wasl on the next breath.

examples.focus: ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ ٱلَّذِىٓ أَنزَلَ عَلَىٰ عَبْدِهِ ٱلْكِتَـٰبَ وَلَمْ يَجْعَل لَّهُۥ عِوَجَا ۜ. The small ۜ is sakta (a brief pause without taking a breath), reminding the reciter not to merge عِوَجَا into the next word قَيِّمًا.
قَالُوا۟ يَـٰوَيْلَنَا مَنۢ بَعَثَنَا مِن مَّرْقَدِنَا ۜ هَـٰذَا. Another classical sakta site.

fragments.caption: sakta mark ۜ: brief silent pause, no breath

lessons.summary: Stopping marks in the mushaf classify each potential pause point. The marks are guides for meaning. A stop in the wrong place can join phrases that should stay separate.

chapters.subtitle: Where you may stop, and what changes when you do
